questions.q: What is the correct order for turning a local capstone folder into a tracked Git repository, before it's ever pushed anywhere?
options: git push, then git commit, then git add, then git init
git init, then git add, then git commit
git commit, then git init, then git add
git remote add origin, then git init
questions.explain: git init starts tracking the folder, git add stages the files you want included, and git commit saves that staged snapshot as the first commit.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does git remote add origin do?
options: It deletes all local commit history
It creates a new branch called main
It points your local repo at a hosted copy — in this lesson, a GitHub repository
It stages every changed file for the next commit
questions.explain: git remote add origin connects your local repository to a hosted remote (GitHub), so git push has somewhere to send your commits.

questions.q: This lesson lists three categories of file that typically belong in this project's .gitignore. Which of these is one of them?
options: Any connection string or credentials file created for local testing
The SSIS package (.dtsx) itself
The README.md file
The T-SQL warehouse DDL
questions.explain: Credentials and connection strings should never be committed — once committed, they're recoverable from the repo's history forever, even after a later commit removes the file.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a .gitignore should be set up before your first commit, rather than added later?
options: GitHub requires a .gitignore to exist before a repo can be created
A .gitignore file only works on Linux, not Windows
.gitignore files slow down git push noticeably
Once a file is committed, it's recoverable from the repo's history forever, even if a later commit deletes it
questions.explain: This directly echoes the Git fundamentals lesson: .gitignore only stops a file from being tracked going forward — it does nothing to scrub something already committed.

questions.q: What does this lesson say a reviewer should be able to do with the SSIS and SQL files in a working portfolio repo?
options: Download a ZIP file and extract it to a separate hard drive before viewing anything
Read them directly on GitHub, with no download required
Request them by email from the repo owner
Install SSIS locally before anything in the repo becomes visible
questions.explain: Part of confirming the repo actually works as evidence is checking that a stranger can read the real files directly on GitHub, with nothing to install or download first.
